Subject: Performance SLO qualification - follow-up & cost levers

Jamie - thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and a few follow-ups so we can size a benchmark and give you realistic cost guidance.

Recap of the targets you shared:
- Latency: p95 <= 200ms for streamed chat responses (streaming is required)
- Sustained throughput: ~150 requests/sec across public endpoints
- Peak concurrency: up to ~100 concurrent sessions with short spikes to 200 for a few minutes
- Typical input length: ~512 tokens, average response ~150 tokens
- Security/compliance: workplace PHI-scope concerns - you flagged that data residency and audit logs matter (we noted Private deployment options).

Primary technical constraints we should validate in the benchmark:
1) End-to-end streaming latency (first token + tail) under p95 SLA
2) Throughput at target concurrency with streaming enabled
3) Impact of caching (prefix/KV) on both latency and token cost

Initial cost/performance levers we recommend exploring (we'll quantify after microbenchmarks):
- Continuous batching: reduces per-token CPU/GPU overhead at modest added input latency; good for steady throughput
- KV/prefix caching: drastic latency and cost wins when prompts share common prefixes (e.g., system prompts, long context)
- Quantization profiles (int8 / mixed precision): major memory and throughput gains; small quality delta for many workloads
- Model variants / routing: use smaller or quantized variants for low-latency paths and fall back to larger models for edge cases
- Adaptive routing & fallback policies: keep availability and SLA during capacity pressure

Attachments: orchid-performance-requirements.xlsx (sample traffic, endpoints, and example payloads). I attached a short PDF with cost levers for reference; Marcus will follow with a technical note.

Next steps:
- Marcus: run microbenchmarks on our near-term candidate configs (quantized Llama-3 13B int8, medium-sized variants, and with/without KV cache) using your sample payloads - target delivery by Fri 3/27.
- Priya: draft procurement checklist and any compliance artifacts you asked for.
- I'll schedule a 60-min architecture call next week to go over results and deployment options.

Does that match what you expected? Anything I missed?

Best,

Looping in a few quick technical notes that will help answer Jamie's ballpark asks. Marcus here - infra lead for the benchmark.

High-level, assuming the workload Marissa summarized (512 token inputs, ~150 token responses, streaming):
- Quantization (int8) alone: expect ~1.6-2x improvement in throughput and ~15-35% reduction in per-token GPU time versus FP16, depending on kernel optimizations. Latency p95 for first token improves slightly because more model fits on GPU RAM enabling higher concurrency.
- KV/prefix caching (30% reuse): can reduce total token decoding by ~20-40% for prefix-heavy flows which translates directly to token cost and to lower tail latency for repeated prompts. This is the biggest easy win if your prompts have common system context.
- Continuous batching (100ms max batch latency): excellent for steady traffic - 20-50% reduction in per-token cost at steady state. For spiky traffic we recommend an adaptive policy: smaller max latency during spikes to protect first-token SLA, larger during steady windows.
- Model variants: at p95 targets, a quantized medium variant (8-13B quantized) often hits sub-200ms p95 for first token in our lab with streaming enabled at ~100 concurrent sessions; a full 13B FP16 will have higher quality but ~1.5x the cost. We'll publish exact numbers from the bench.

Ballpark cost deltas (very rough):
A) Quantization only (int8) vs FP16: ~20-40% cost reduction per token depending on GPU type and kernel stack.
B) KV caching (30% reuse): additional ~15-30% effective cost reduction (depends on how much response generation is avoided).
C) Continuous batching (100ms max) vs no batching: ~20-40% cost reduction at steady-state traffic.

Caveats: these are top-level ranges. Real results depend on GPU type (A100 vs H100 vs T4-class), sequence-length distributions, and the fraction of responses that are cacheable. We'll use your sample payloads to nail the numbers.

I'll run the bench on NGC-optimized runtime + quantized kernels and attach the raw results. Expect a first pass by 2026-03-27.

Attaching: redwood-slo-cost-levers.pdf (short technical appendix).

- Marcus
